name: Orbital rim implants

lead: Orbital rim implants are synthetic implants placed on the bony rim under the eye to reduce hollowing and support the lower lid, giving a smoother, more supported under-eye. They are sometimes combined with cheek (malar) implants. Hardmaxxing forums discuss them as a durable alternative to filler.

A silicone, porous polyethylene or similar implant, standard or custom-made from CT scans, is placed under the periosteum of the rim and secured, adding projection to the bony support. Published data on cosmetic use are limited, and much of the satisfaction data comes from malar implants.

paras: It is a surgical procedure done under anaesthesia by a facial surgeon, with recovery of several weeks. Forum discussion centres on standard versus custom designs and on pairing with cheek implants.

Reported complications include lower eyelid malposition, infection, contour irregularities and implant extrusion, and rarely nerve injury or sinus fistula. It is major facial surgery, so people with active infection or unrealistic expectations are typically advised against it.

angle.text: Implants along the lower orbital rim build bony support under the eye and smooth hollows and tear troughs, a change you can see once healed. It is promoted as more durable than fillers. Published data on cosmetic use is thin.

lead: Infraorbital or orbital rim implants are alloplastic (synthetic) devices placed along the lower orbital rim to add bony support under the eye. Grokipedia describes them as typically made of medical-grade silicone, intended for tear trough hollows, rim recession and a negative orbital vector, and presented as a more durable alternative to fillers or fat grafting [1].

Published evidence is limited. Grokipedia states that large studies of infraorbital implants are scarce and cites satisfaction figures mainly from malar implant series [1]. In looksmaxxing forums the implants are discussed, often alongside malar implants, as a hardmaxxing option for eye-area support, with debate over standard versus custom designs.

paras: According to Grokipedia, solid silicone is inert and encapsulated by scar tissue, while porous polyethylene allows tissue ingrowth and is typically screw-fixed [1]. Standard implants are prefabricated for milder cases; custom implants are built from a patient's CT data and may extend into the cheek area; combined implants address both the under-eye and cheek [1].

The implant is described as placed in a pocket beneath the periosteum through a conjunctival, intraoral or lower-eyelid approach, protecting the infraorbital nerve and secured with sutures or screws [1]. Swelling and bruising are reported to improve over one to three weeks, with activity restrictions of about two weeks [1].

Grokipedia reports a 10-patient series with about three years of follow-up showing stable results without infection or nerve damage, and notes that larger satisfaction data come from malar implants [1]. Reported complications include lower eyelid malposition, infection, contour irregularities and extrusion, with rarer nerve injury, lacrimal sac penetration and sinus fistula [1]. This source is AI-generated and has not been independently verified.

No clinical studies on cosmetic infraorbital rim implants were found. Related work includes a 1999 cadaver-skull study on lateral orbital rim implants to expand orbital volume in thyroid eye disease [2], and registered trials of custom PEEK cranial implants, which concern a different indication [3].

Forum users compare infraorbital rim and malar implants, with some stating that off-the-shelf malar implants add too much lower-face volume and that custom implants are needed for men. Others post results and question whether implants altered the cheek contour.
